resources.string: SnapKey Mapper is listening: %1$d press(es) detected
Three switches, once. The key itself needs nothing else.

Join your Wi-Fi, tap the button, then in Developer options turn on Wireless debugging, tap \"Pair device with pairing code\" and type the 6 digits in the notification. On ColorOS, turn on \"Disable system optimisation\" first.
On ColorOS, also set Battery usage to \"No restrictions\" in the app settings and lock the app in the recent apps.
A web address, a deep link or an intent: link
Single press is the fastest; a double press never fires from a press in your pocket. A change applies at once.

The Find X9 key is already known. On another phone: start the capture, press the side key 2 or 3 times, stop, then tap the line that comes back at every press. The capture can contain personal information from other apps: check it before sharing it.
Save the capture to a file
Pattern to recognise (part of the line, without numbers that change)

No line: tick \"Show all lines\" or check the permission
Choose the pattern first (menu › Another phone)
Press the side key to open your target

In Developer options, turn on Wireless debugging and tap \"Pair device with pairing code\"
Pull the notification down and write the 6 digits shown by Android

Phone\'s own Snap Key action off
Done: the Snap Key does nothing on its own
The Find X9 key is already known: nothing to do here. On another phone, the app has to learn which line Android writes in its log when you press your key.

string-array.name: steps_log_auto
string-array.item: Connect the phone to your Wi-Fi.
If Developer options are hidden: Settings › About device › Version, tap the build number 7 times.
In Developer options, turn on \"Disable system optimisation\" (ColorOS).
Tap \"Set up log reading automatically\" below.
Turn Wireless debugging on, then tap \"Pair device with pairing code\".
Pull the notifications down and type the 6 digits in the SnapKey Mapper notification.

string-array.name: steps_log_computer
string-array.item: On a computer, install Android platform-tools (adb).
In Developer options, turn on USB debugging and \"Disable system optimisation\" (ColorOS), then connect the phone with a cable.
Run the command below on the computer.

string-array.name: steps_overlay
string-array.item: Tap \"Open the setting\" and turn the switch on.
If the switch is grey or Android says access is denied: tap \"Open the app settings\", then ⋮ at the top right › \"Allow restricted settings\", then come back here.

string-array.name: steps_battery
string-array.item: Tap \"Allow\" and confirm.
On ColorOS, also open the app settings › Battery usage › \"No restrictions\", and lock the app in the recent apps.

string-array.name: steps_native
string-array.item: Open the phone settings and search for \"Snap Key\".
Set it to no action, so the phone does not run its own action at the same time.
Tick the box below.

string-array.name: steps_finder
string-array.item: Tap \"Start capture\".
Press your key 3 times, a few seconds apart.
Tap \"Stop capture\".
In the list below, tap the line that came back at each press: it becomes the pattern.
Go back home, start listening and press the key to check.

resources.string: Not working on your phone? On a computer, ask Claude Code with the SnapKey Mapper plugin: it finds a link that works and tests it on your phone, connected with a USB cable or wireless debugging.
The app gives itself the log permission through the phone\'s wireless debugging, which only works on Wi-Fi. Connect the phone, then come back here.
Tap the button, then tap the build number 7 times (on ColorOS: Version). Android says you are a developer. Come back here.
Pair the app with your phone

1. Tap the button: Wireless debugging opens (if the Developer options list opens instead, tap the text "Wireless debugging", not the switch).
2. Turn on "Use wireless debugging" and allow your network.
3. Tap "Pair device with pairing code".
4. A SnapKey Mapper notification drops down: tap its arrow to unfold it, tap "Enter code" and type the 6 digits. That is all, the app does the rest.

ColorOS blocks the permission until a hidden switch is on, and it only shows when the phone is in English.
1. Switch the phone to English (Language & region).
2. In Settings, search "Disable system" and turn on "Disable system optimisation" (Turn on anyway).
3. Come back here. After the setup you can put your language back.
The lite edition has no network access, so the permission is given from a computer, once: turn on USB debugging in Developer options, connect the phone with a cable and run this command.
Lets the key open your target even when the screen is off or another app is in front. Tap the button, then SnapKey Mapper in the list, and turn the switch on.

Switch greyed out, or \"access denied\"? Android blocks it for apps installed from outside the Play Store: open the app settings, tap ⋮ at the top right, then \"Allow restricted settings\", and come back.
So that Android does not stop the app in the background. Tap the button and confirm. On ColorOS, also lock the app in the recent apps.
So that the phone does not run its own Snap Key action at the same time: in the phone settings, search for \"Snap Key\" and set it to no action.
All set. The key now listens by itself. You can turn Wireless debugging off. Choose what the key opens.
A few steps, once. The app opens each setting for you and checks it.
The key does nothing? Another phone: find your key
The pairing code is typed in a notification of the app. Turn on its notifications, then come back here.
Diagnostic copied: paste it in a GitHub issue
